title: What a language model actually is
s: A language model is a function that predicts the next piece of text. Everything else, from chat to code, is built on top of that one trick.
x: start with a game. read "the capital of france is" and guess the next word. you said "paris" without effort, and you were right because you have seen that sentence completed many times before. a language model plays exactly this game, at enormous scale. given some text, it outputs a probability for every possible next piece of text. "paris" gets a high one. "banana" gets a tiny one. that is the whole job description. text so far | "the capital of france is" model | a very large function next-piece probabilities | paris 92%, the 2%, a 1%, … pick one | sample or take the most likely ## one step at a time a model does not write a paragraph at once. it predicts one piece, adds it to the text, and predicts again. a chat reply of 300 words is hundreds of these small steps in a row, each one conditioned on everything written so far, including the model's own earlier output. this is why the same

title: Tokens: how text becomes numbers
s: Models read and write tokens, not words. Tokens decide what you pay for, how much fits in context, and why models stumble on spelling and arithmetic.
x: a neural network only does arithmetic on numbers, so text has to be turned into numbers before a model can touch it. the first step is to cut the text into pieces. each piece gets an integer id, and that id later becomes a list of numbers the model can work with. the pieces are called tokens, and the program that cuts text into them is the tokenizer. ## why not words, and why not letters splitting on whole words sounds natural, but it breaks quickly. a word list large enough to cover every name, typo, code identifier and language would be enormous, and any word not on the list would be unreadable. splitting into single characters or bytes fixes that, because every text can be spelled out. but the sequences get very long, and the model has to spend effort re-learning that "t", "h", "e" belong together. subword tokenization sits in between. common words stay whole. rare words are built fro

title: Attention and the transformer
s: Attention lets each token look back at earlier tokens and decide which ones matter. Stacked many times, it is the core of every modern language model.
x: after tokenization, a model holds a row of integer ids. the transformer, introduced in the paper attention is all you need, is the machine that turns that row into a prediction for the next token. its central idea is attention. ## embeddings: a list of numbers per token each token id is looked up in a table and replaced by a list of numbers called an embedding. these lists are learned during training. tokens that are used in similar ways end up with similar lists. at this point each token still knows nothing about its neighbours: "bank" has the same embedding in "river bank" and "bank loan". ## attention: which earlier words matter meaning depends on context. in "the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big", the word "it" refers to the trophy. to process "it", the model needs to look back and find "trophy". attention does exactly that. for each token, it scores every ea

title: How a model learns
s: Training is a loop that measures how surprised the model was by real text and nudges its parameters to be less surprised next time.
x: before training, a model's parameters are random numbers, and its predictions are noise. after training, the same architecture writes fluent text. nothing changes in between except the values of those parameters. this lesson is about how they get adjusted. take a batch | chunks of real text predict | probabilities for each next token measure loss | how surprised was the model? update | nudge every parameter slightly ## loss: how surprised was the model for every position in the text, the model gives a probability to the token that actually came next. the loss turns that into one number. in cross-entropy loss, it is the negative logarithm of the probability given to the right answer. in plain words: how surprised was the model by what really happened. the real next token was "paris". model gave it 90%: loss = -ln(0.9) = 0.11 model gave it 50%: loss = -ln(0.5) = 0.69 model gave it 1%: loss

title: Pretraining data
s: Frontier models read tens of trillions of tokens, but most of the raw web is thrown away first. Quality, mixture and repetition shape what the model learns.
x: a model can only learn from what it reads. for a frontier model, that is somewhere between 27 and 48 trillion tokens of text, code and now images and audio. how that pile is collected, cleaned and mixed has a large effect on the result, and labs publish less about it than about the architecture. glm-5 | 28.5 | all stages mimo-v2.6-pro | 30 | 27t text plus 3t omni deepseek-v4-pro | 33 | a summary figure, check the paper inkling | 45 | secondary source mimo-v2.6-flash | 48 | 26t text plus 22t omni ## where the text comes from the largest source is the web. crawlers collect billions of pages, and the raw html is turned into text by extraction: removing menus, ads and boilerplate and keeping the main content. open projects such as fineweb show this pipeline in public. beyond the web, labs use books, scientific papers, code repositories and, for multimodal models, images, video and speech tra

title: Scaling laws: how big, how long
s: Loss falls smoothly as parameters, data and compute grow. Scaling laws turn that into a budgeting tool, and also show where the tool stops working.
x: before a lab spends months and tens of millions of dollars on a training run, it has to answer two questions. how many parameters should the model have? and how much text should it read? guessing wrong in either direction wastes money. scaling laws are the empirical rules that make the guess an informed one. ## loss falls on a smooth curve during training a model is scored by its loss, a number that measures how badly it predicts the next token (lower is better). in 2020, kaplan and colleagues trained many models of different sizes and found something tidy. loss followed a power law in three quantities: the number of parameters, the amount of training data, and the amount of compute. plotted on log axes, the results fell close to a straight line over many orders of magnitude. the practical meaning is that progress is predictable. train a few small models, fit the line, and you can foreca

title: Parameters, precision and memory
s: A parameter is a stored number, and every number costs bytes. Precision, gradients and optimizer state decide whether a model fits on one chip or needs a cluster.
x: saying a model has 70 billion parameters sounds abstract. physically it means 70 billion numbers sitting in memory, and each number occupies a fixed number of bytes. multiply the two and you know whether the model fits on your hardware. ## a parameter is a stored number a parameter is one adjustable number in the model, usually a weight inside a large matrix. training changes these numbers a little at a time. using the model only reads them. how much space each one takes depends on its precision, the number of bits used to write it down. fp32 | 4 | 32 bits, the traditional default bf16 | 2 | 16 bits, common for training and serving fp8 | 1 | 8 bits 4-bit (fp4, int4) | 0.5 | plus a small overhead for scales bf16 keeps the same range of values as fp32 but with fewer digits of detail. that trade works well for neural networks, which tolerate a little noise in each weight. ## why a 70b model

title: GPUs and parallelism
s: A GPU is fast only when its arithmetic units stay fed. Training a large model means splitting it across thousands of GPUs in several ways at once, and paying for the communication.
x: a modern training run uses thousands of gpus working as one machine. to see why, and why that is hard, start with a single chip. ## how a gpu runs work a gpu is built from many small processors that run the same instruction on different data. nvidia's h100 has 132 streaming multiprocessors, and each one runs threads in groups of 32 called warps. each multiprocessor has its own fast on-chip memory (228 kb of shared memory usable on the h100), while the large main memory, hbm, sits off to the side. the h100 sxm has 80 gb of hbm at 3.35 tb/s. for matrix multiplication, the part that dominates language models, gpus have special tensor cores. on the h100, dense bf16 math on tensor cores peaks at about 989 tflops, roughly 15 times the 67 tflops of its ordinary fp32 units. those peak figures are for dense math; nvidia's headline numbers are often doubled by counting sparsity. ## compute-bound o

title: Mixture of experts
s: A mixture-of-experts model stores many specialist sub-networks but sends each token to only a few. It gets the capacity of a huge model at the arithmetic cost of a much smaller one.
x: most of the largest 2026 models share one design choice. they are mixtures of experts, or moe. understanding it explains why their parameter counts come in two numbers. ## dense and sparse in a dense model, every parameter takes part in processing every token. doubling the parameters roughly doubles the arithmetic per token. in a sparse moe model, the feed-forward part of each layer is replaced by many parallel sub-networks called experts. for each token, only a few experts run. the rest sit idle for that token. the attention layers stay shared, as in the transformer. token arrives | one piece of text in a layer router | scores every expert top experts | a few are chosen, such as 8 combine | their outputs are mixed by score ## the router the router is a small learned layer. it takes the token's representation and produces a score for each expert. the highest scores win, and the token is

title: When training breaks
s: At frontier scale something is always failing. How labs survive broken chips, loss spikes, silent wrong answers and fragile low-precision numbers.
x: a training run for a frontier model keeps thousands of chips busy for weeks or months. each chip, cable, memory module and software library has some small chance of failing on any given day. multiply a small chance by a very large number of parts and failure stops being an exception. it becomes a routine event that the whole system has to be designed around. ## hardware fails all the time a january 2026 paper from meta and partners measured this on a job with 32,000 gpus. they saw 2.3 interruptions per 1,000 servers per day, and 78% of them were hardware related. even so, the job spent 95 to 97% of its time making real progress. that number is the effective training time: the share of wall-clock time that actually moves the model forward, rather than waiting, restarting or redoing lost work. scale changes the picture quickly. for a job on 100,000 gpus, the same paper estimates a failure

title: Supervised fine-tuning
s: How a raw text predictor becomes an assistant by studying examples of good answers, and why a small, clean dataset can beat a large, messy one.
x: a freshly pre-trained model is a powerful text predictor, but it is not yet an assistant. ask it "what is the capital of france?" and it may continue with "what is the capital of germany?", because lists of quiz questions are common in its training text. it is completing a document, not answering you. supervised fine-tuning, usually shortened to sft, closes that gap. the model is trained further on examples of the behaviour we want: a request followed by a good reply. the training signal is the same one used in pre-training, predict the next token, only the text is now different. ## instruction data an instruction dataset is a collection of pairs. each has a prompt (a question, a task, a conversation so far) and a target response written to be the ideal answer. the responses come from people, from other models, or from a mix, with humans reviewing the results. the frontier training film

title: Preference tuning and reinforcement learning
s: How models learn from comparisons and from checkable rewards: RLHF, DPO, verifiable rewards, group-based RL, and the sandboxes and reward hacking that come with it.
x: after supervised fine-tuning, a model imitates good answers. imitation has a ceiling: the model cannot easily become better than its examples, and for many tasks it is hard to write the ideal answer but easy to say which of two answers is better, or whether an answer is simply right. reinforcement learning uses exactly that kind of feedback. in reinforcement learning (rl), the model generates an attempt, a reward scores it, and the model's weights are adjusted to make high-scoring attempts more likely. the model's behaviour is called its policy. prompt | a task or question rollout | the model writes an attempt reward | a score for the attempt update | good attempts become more likely ## rlhf in plain steps reinforcement learning from human feedback (rlhf) is the method behind instructgpt. it works in three steps. 1. collect comparisons. for a prompt, the model writes several answers and

title: Evaluation
s: How we measure what a model can do, and why every measurement has a catch: contamination, saturation, judge bias and scores that cannot be compared across versions.
x: training produces a model. evaluation tells you what you actually got. it sounds like the easy part, and it is among the hardest, because a language model can do an open-ended range of things and any test samples only a few of them. ## what a benchmark measures a benchmark is a fixed set of tasks with a way to score the answers. mmlu, for example, is a large collection of multiple-choice questions across many school and professional subjects, scored by accuracy. coding benchmarks give the model a task and run the resulting code against tests. agent benchmarks give it a computer-like environment and check whether the job got done. the frontier training film shows what current reports look like. deepseek v4 pro, in its maximum reasoning mode, reports 80.6 on swe-bench verified and 67.9 on terminal bench 2.0. the test setup is itself an engineering system: those agent tests allow up to 500

title: Distillation and quantization
s: Two ways to make a model cheaper to run: teach a small model to imitate a big one, or store the same weights in fewer bits. What each one keeps, and what it costs.
x: a trained model is expensive to run mostly because it is big. there are two direct ways to shrink the bill. you can build a smaller model that behaves like the large one, which is distillation. or you can keep the model as it is and store each number with fewer bits, which is quantization. they attack different things, and modern models often use both. ## distillation: a student that imitates a teacher in distillation, a large, strong teacher model is used to train a smaller student. the idea comes from hinton and colleagues in 2015. the key observation is about what the teacher's output contains. when a model predicts the next token, it produces a full probability distribution, not just a winner. if the right answer is "cat", a good teacher may give "dog" a small but real probability and "carburettor" almost none. that pattern of near-misses says something about how the world is organis

title: Inference and sampling
s: How a trained model produces text: a fast reading phase, a slow one-token-at-a-time writing phase, a memory called the KV cache, and the sampling rules that pick each token.
x: inference means using a trained model to produce output. training happens once, at great expense. inference happens every time anyone sends a prompt, so its cost adds up, and the way it works shapes everything from response speed to price. ## two phases: prefill and decode every request has two stages. in prefill, the model reads your whole prompt at once. all the prompt's tokens can be processed in parallel, so the chip does large matrix multiplications and stays busy. in decode, the model writes its answer one token at a time. each new token needs a full pass through the network, and it cannot start until the previous token exists. prompt arrives | thousands of tokens at once prefill | parallel, compute-heavy decode | one token per pass, repeated stop | end token or length limit ## why decoding is limited by memory bandwidth during decode, each pass reads essentially every active weigh

title: What "open" means for AI models
s: "Open" can mean downloadable weights, public code, released data or a full training recipe. These are different things, with different freedoms, and few releases include all four.
x: when a model is called "open", the word covers at least four separate things. which one is meant changes what you are allowed to do, and what you can check for yourself. recall from what a language model actually is that a model, stored on disk, is a very large list of numbers. that is the starting point for the first kind of openness. ## four things that can be open ## open weights - the trained numbers can be downloaded - you can run the model on your own hardware - you can often fine-tune it ## open code - the code to run, and sometimes train, the model is published - lets others reproduce the setup ## open data - the training data, or exact recipes to rebuild it, is released - lets others inspect what the model learned from ## open recipe - the settings, stages and tricks of training are described - lets others repeat or improve the method open weights is the most common meaning toda

title: How a base model is trained, end to end
s: Every step from raw text to a base model, followed through one real model, the OpenEuroLLM 9B that sits under Agora, with interactive demos of the loss, the optimizer, the schedule and long context.
x: a base model is what you get when a network has read an enormous amount of text and learned to predict what comes next. it is not yet an assistant. ask it a question and it may continue with another question, because lists of questions are common in text. everything that makes a model useful comes later, in post-training. but the base model decides what is possible, so most of the cost, risk and engineering sits here. this guide follows one real model all the way through: the openeurollm 9b base that agora 9b was built on. we use it because its model card publishes the architecture, the training stages, the optimizer settings and the run's health in unusual detail. a caveat up front: the card documents the long-context continuation of the model in full, but describes the earlier pre-training only by name and size. where we explain the general recipe, we say so. where a number comes from

title: How a base model becomes an assistant, end to end
s: Seven stages of post-training followed through one real model, Agora 9B, with its data, recipes, costs and scores, and interactive demos of loss masking, preference tuning, weight merging and reinforcement learning.
x: a base model predicts text. an assistant answers questions, follows instructions, reasons step by step when asked, calls tools, behaves safely and stops when it is done. the distance between the two is covered by post-training, which is a sequence of stages rather than one trick, and each stage fixes something the last one left or broke. this guide follows one real model, agora 9b, through all of them. agora is a multilingual assistant for european languages with an opt-in thinking mode and tool calling. its model card records the whole pipeline unusually openly: data, recipe, compute and the score after every stage, including a stage that made things worse. that is what makes it a good teaching case. numbers on this page come from the card unless they are marked as illustrations. instruct sft | learn to answer reasoning sft | learn to think first tool-use sft | learn to call tools dpo |

title: Keeping AI agents safe: injection, incidents and design
s: Why agents raise the stakes over chatbots, how prompt injection works, real incidents, and the design rules and habits that limit the damage.
x: prompt injection and rules that limit damage an agent can act, so a wrong action has already happened. the film explains prompt injection, reviews real incidents, and presents two design rules, the lethal trifecta and meta's rule of two. it argues that safety must be built into the surrounding system, and covers least privilege, sandboxes, separating trusted from untrusted input and human approval. a language model cannot reliably tell an instruction from you apart from an instruction hidden in content it reads, which is prompt injection. the lethal trifecta is private data, untrusted content and a way to send information out; an agent should have at most two of three. the film reports attacks on anthropic's browser agent worked about one time in four without defenses and about one in nine with safeguards. safety cannot rely only on the model saying no, so least privilege, sandboxes and separating trusted from untrusted input matter. keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible, such as sending, paying, deleting or publishing, and keep backups. intro prompt injection real incidents the lethal trifecta the rule of two security engineering answers separating trusted input habits and closing

title: Post-training a European model, stage by stage
s: A walkthrough of turning a raw 9-billion-parameter European base model into an assistant, with the bugs, evaluations and fixes found at each stage.
x: what worked, what broke and how we found out the film follows the post-training of open euro llm, a 9-billion-parameter model, on the leonardo supercomputer. it covers instruction tuning, a thinking mode, tool use, preference training and reinforcement learning, and shows what each stage broke, how it was caught by evaluation, and how it was fixed, including by merging weights. post-training is a pipeline of stages, and the same evaluations run between stages so each step's gains and damage are visible. the film reports that unclosed tool calls came from nearly identical output weights on new tag tokens, fixed by refitting eight rows. data teaches exactly what it contains: the speaker found that 99% of strict-format training answers ignored the format. reinforcement learning can only reinforce what the model already does sometimes, so rewards need partial credit the model can climb. averaging the weights of two models from the same parent can restore a skill lost in a later stage. intro chat template instruction tuning thinking mode tool use preference training merging weights reinforcement learning combined rl run closing

title: Envy is a compass
s: Envy is not proof that you are a bad friend. It is precise, and it points at what you still want.
x: what the sting of comparison points at you do not envy everything, only the things you want. this film looks at why other people's good news can make you sink, the two kinds of envy researchers describe, and a way to read the feeling instead of hiding it. it ends with a small dare for one week. envy is precise: it does not point at what is impressive, it points at what you want. researchers describe two kinds, one that pulls the other person down and one that pulls you up. ask what exactly stung, and whether you want the thing or want to be seen having it. studies of good news find that an enthusiastic response builds trust and closeness between people. a small step toward the thing, even twenty minutes, tells the compass you are listening. 11:47 pm envy is precise why it is so loud the two kinds of envy how to read it why not me? not yet what you get back a dare for this week closing sources

title: The mind is a machine that makes up stories
s: The mind turns what happens into stories about you and the world. Seeing them as stories makes room for other, more accurate ones.
x: why a sad day turns into a sad story a short talk on how the mind makes sense of the world by telling stories. those stories are not always accurate, and a bad day can easily become a story about who you are. once you see the pattern, you can ask what is really going on and choose a more flexible story. everything you experience passes through the unconscious mind and then through personal models, such as models for language and for how you perceive sound. the mind works to make sense of things, and a story that makes sense can win out over one that is accurate. a bad day can turn into a story about yourself or the world, such as that you are a failure or that nothing works. a more accurate story is often practical, for example that you feel sad because you skipped exercise or have not seen friends. you will not stop making stories, but you can hold them more loosely and ask what you can do instead. intro how stories get made sense before truth a more accurate story stories, not facts holding stories flexibly

title: What is intelligence?
s: A short essay in film: intelligence as finding and keeping the right pattern, and how brains and language models share that shape.
x: compression, direction and two kinds of mind the film asks what a mind does that a rock does not. its answer is that a mind finds patterns, compresses the world, keeps what matters and updates from error. it then looks at direction and honesty, compares a human brain with a language model, and ends with a mind that models itself. predicting and compressing are two views of the same act, because the better you predict, the less you have to remember. compression is never neutral: what a mind keeps depends on what it wants. the real test of intelligence is a problem it has never seen, where memory has no entry. a language model trained to predict text is trained to compress it, and what it carries is that compression. both humans and models can fail at updating, one by resisting change and the other by giving way to pressure. the question finding the pattern what you keep the unseen problem the loop direction two minds turning inward

title: The alignment problem: whose values should AI follow?
s: How assistants learn behavior from human choices, four questions where reasonable people disagree, and the ways ordinary people can take part.
x: human feedback, hard choices and how to take part the film explains alignment as closing the gap between a capable model and one that is helpful, honest and harmless. it covers learning from human feedback and what went wrong when a model became flattering. it then walks through four open questions, the problem of whose values count, and concrete ways people can take part. a pretrained model is capable but does not know which of its possible answers people actually want, and alignment closes that gap. the film describes a 2025 rollback of an overly flattering update, and draws the lesson that what we reward is what we get. medical advice, privacy, reporting users and whose side the model is on are dials that someone must set for every model. the film argues that written values such as constitutions and specifications can be debated and improved, while hidden values cannot. people can take part by voting, rating honestly, joining deliberations, reviewing tests in their own language and speaking up when rules are written. intro capable is not aligned learning from feedback four hard questions reporting users whose side is it on whose values written values and taking part closing

title: Why AI makes things up and how to guard against it
s: Why language models state invented facts with confidence, how a model can learn to say it does not know, and what you can do to protect yourself.
x: hallucination, calibration and checking the film opens with real cases where invented ai output caused harm. it explains why models hallucinate, including rare facts and benchmarks that reward guessing, introduces calibration and semantic entropy, and looks at retrieval and citations and their limits. it ends with practical habits for checking ai answers. a model trained to continue text in a plausible way can produce the right form of an answer with an invented fact inside. the film argues that benchmarks scoring i don't know as zero reward confident guessing, so scoring should penalize confident wrong answers more. calibration means that when a model is 90% sure, it should be right about nine times out of ten. retrieval and citations help but do not guarantee truth, so you still need to click the link and read the passage. be especially careful with names, numbers, dates, quotes and references, and confirm high-stakes answers with a person or original source. intro why models make things up guessing and benchmarks calibration telling when it guesses retrieval and citations limits of retrieval how to protect yourself closing

title: Where the silicon ends
s: Why Hopper cannot run 4-bit math at full speed and Blackwell can, and which GPU limits are carved in silicon rather than code.
x: what a gpu limits and what software can change hopper has no 4-bit tensor cores and blackwell does. the film separates what is fixed in silicon from what software can still change. it covers how a gpu runs work, the roofline model, dense tensor formats for nvidia and amd, 4-bit weights on hopper, native nvfp4 training and the cuda and rocm software layer. a tensor core is fixed hardware, reached only through instructions that list the number formats it supports. decoding one token at a time is memory bound, while large-batch training is compute bound, and a number format affects each differently. four-bit weights on hopper cut memory traffic about four times, but the multiply still runs in 16 bits. on blackwell b200, dense 4-bit peak is twice 8-bit, and on b300 it is three times. software can change how many bytes move and how close you get to the roofline, but it cannot raise the roofline. intro how a gpu runs work compute bound or memory bound what fixed silicon means why tricks fall short nvidia generations amd generations hardware limits and software 4-bit weights on hopper native nvfp4 training block scales and fp8 the software layer recap sources

title: How AI agents work: build one from scratch
s: Builds an agent piece by piece: a model that predicts text, a context list, tools, a loop, then memory, skills, sub-agents and autonomy.
x: model, context, tools and a loop the film builds an agent from nothing. it starts with a model that only predicts tokens, shows that a chatbot's memory is a list the program resends, and adds tools and a loop. it then covers context limits and compaction, memory, skills, sub-agents, heartbeats for autonomy, and the safety risks that come with more power. a language model only predicts the next token; a chatbot's memory is a message list that the program sends again every time. giving the model tool descriptions lets it ask the program to act, and a loop of ask, act and ask again makes an agent. the context holds everything and is resent every step, so agents compact older parts, and deciding what to keep is the art. skills load full instructions only when a task matches, and sub-agents return only a short report to keep the main context clean. more power means more risk, so treat what an agent reads as data, give least access and ask a human before irreversible steps. intro context and tools the agent loop a real run context and compaction memory skills and sub-agents autonomy and risk closing

title: Memory is an experience
s: Each time you remember, you rebuild the memory in the present, which means the way you see the past can change.
x: why remembering is rebuilding, not replaying a memory is not a file you open. it is rebuilt each time you recall it, from old pieces and present understanding. the film walks through the evidence, from bartlett to reconsolidation, and shows how distance and warmth can shift what we see, without inventing what happened. remembering is rebuilding: the pieces are old, but the scene is assembled new each time. a single word in a question can reshape what people remember, which is how memory normally works. when a memory is recalled it briefly becomes open to updating, though scientists are still mapping when and how. reinterpreting is not inventing: the events stay the same, and understanding someone is not excusing them. confidence is not accuracy, so the aim is a truer story held with curiosity, not one that only feels good. intro remembering is rebuilding one word changes memory memories reopen when recalled retelling shapes memory two readings of one moment wise feedback shifting the lens a word of care a gentle practice closing sources

title: Running on empty: understanding burnout
s: If you wake up already tired, you may not be lazy. Burnout has a shape that research describes, and five steps that help you come back.
x: what it is, why it happens, five steps back burnout is what happens after a long time under more pressure than you can recover from. the film explains its three parts and why it arises when work takes more than it gives back. it then walks through five steps: stop the drain, change the load, change the voice in your head, rebuild the basics and lean on other people. researchers describe burnout as exhaustion, cynicism and feeling less effective, after long pressure without enough recovery. in the demands and resources model, burnout is usually a mismatch: too much going out and too little coming in, for too long. programs aimed at the organization, such as workload and teamwork, tended to work better than programs aimed at the individual. psychological detachment, leaving work in your head as well as in your evenings, is the most studied recovery skill. withdrawing usually makes burnout heavier, and telling one person the real answer is a way to start. you used to care what burnout is why it happens step 1: stop the drain step 2: change the load step 3: your inner voice step 4: rebuild basics step 5: other people a week to begin closing sources

title: How reinforcement learning scales for language models
s: How labs run reinforcement learning at production scale: the algorithms, the environments and rewards, the infrastructure and the failure modes.
x: rewards, environments and infrastructure reinforcement learning is described as a second scaling axis after pre-training. the film walks through the basic loop, verifiable rewards, group-based algorithms such as grpo, the environments that score model answers, reward hacking, and the asynchronous systems needed to run it. it compares production runs with the speaker's own small runs. every large rl system repeats one loop: generate a group of answers, score them in an environment, and make the better ones more likely. rewards that a program can check, such as correct math answers or passing tests, are what made today's reasoning models possible. the film reports that about two thirds of the speaker's sampled groups gave no learning signal because every answer was wrong. any reward that can be checked can also be gamed, so hardened environments matter as much as clever algorithms. most of rl training time goes to generating answers, so production systems are built around asynchronous inference. intro the basic rl loop verifiable rewards grpo without a critic multi-stage pipelines environments judges and rubrics reward hacking infrastructure closing

title: Looking inside AI: the science of interpretability
s: How researchers look inside neural networks: superposition, sparse autoencoders, features, circuit tracing, and what this may mean for safety.
x: from single neurons to features and circuits the film explains why individual neurons are hard to read, how superposition packs many concepts into few neurons, and how sparse autoencoders unpack them into features. it then covers steering with features, tracing circuits, links to hallucination, safety uses, and an honest account of how little of a model these methods explain so far. single neurons are confusing because the film says models pack many concepts into overlapping directions, an idea called superposition. sparse autoencoders rewrite a model's activity as a short list of features from a much larger dictionary, each easier to name. turning a feature up changes what the model says, as in the golden gate claude demonstration, which suggests features cause behavior. the film reports that circuit tracing revealed planning ahead in rhymes and an intermediate texas step before answering austin. the film stresses that even in the best studies these methods capture only a small fraction of what a model computes. intro neurons and superposition sparse autoencoders features in large models steering and circuits planning and hallucination languages share circuits safety uses limits today closing
